title: The Boon That Tested Its Own Giver
story:
An asura had chased a god out of the heavens, and now he stood at the gates of Vaikuntha, bellowing, while the god he hunted crouched somewhere within, waiting for the end his own compassion had made possible.

A little while earlier, Vrikasura, son of Shakuni, had tormented himself with penance for seven days and nights until Shiva, the most compassionate of gods, appeared before him and offered him any gift. The asura chose with care: whoever's head he touched would die. The moment the words were spoken, he began to wonder whether the boon was true — and he decided to test it on the head of the very god who had given it. Terrified, Shiva fled across the earth and through the heavens, and the gods looked on helpless, unable to think of any remedy, until at last he stumbled into Vaikuntha, the abode of Vishnu, who never turns away anyone who comes pursued.

The exhausted asura found no terror waiting for him there. Instead a young brahmachari came out to meet him, radiant as a low fire, carrying the staff and deerskin of a wandering student, his face mild and open, as though fear had never touched him. He greeted Vrikasura by name and asked why he looked so spent, and where a victor like him was rushing.

Vrikasura, worn out and vain, told him everything: the penance, the boon, and how he meant to test its truth on Shiva's own head. The young man listened, and a kindly doubt creased his brow.

"Forgive me," he said, "but that cannot be. I have heard that the great god is compassionate, but even compassion has its limits. Such a power, given to an asura, over life itself? No. You have been deceived, or you deceive yourself."

The asura swore it was true. The brahmachari shook his head, still gentle, still smiling. "Then you have nothing to fear from proving it," he said. "Place your hand on your own head. If you live, the tale was always a tale. If you do not — well, then the boon was real after all."

It was said so smoothly, so kindly, that the words seemed to take the breath out of the asura's rage. He had spent his whole chase wanting to prove his power, and here at last was a listener who doubted it. He forgot Shiva. He forgot everything but the insult of being disbelieved. He raised his hand and brought it down on his own head.

The skull split. Vrikasura dropped where he stood, dead in the instant, slain by the very power he had meant to aim at a god.

For a moment Vaikuntha was still. Then flowers rained down from every direction, released by the gods who had watched, helpless, from the edges of the sky. And Shiva, freed at last, stepped out from his hiding and stood before Vishnu, and praised him as the deliverer of the great from those who offend them.

"O Lord," he said, "what creature that has wronged the great has ever survived? This one offended against a god, and his own gift destroyed him. He was never killed by you; he was killed by what he carried."

Vishnu received the praise the way he received everything — quietly, without claiming it. The terror that had emptied the heavens was over. Shiva rested again in Vaikuntha before returning to his own mountain, and the asura's body lay where it had fallen, a lesson in the shape of a corpse: a boon is only as safe as the hand that holds it.
reflection: Vishnu wins without lifting a weapon, by letting the asura's own boon answer for him. There is an exactness to the justice: the power Vrikasura meant to aim at a god had been aimed at himself from the moment he received it, and the gentlest of disguises carried the heaviest of truths.
content_note: A demon dies when his own hand splits his skull; the moment is described with restraint.
next_story_tease: The question that had opened the tale still stood, and the sages would soon put the three great gods themselves to the test.
hero_scene: A radiant young brahmachari with staff and deerskin standing calmly before the towering asura Vrikasura, whose hand is raised to his own head, while flowers fall from a sky full of watching gods and the freed Shiva looks on.
